COLS = ['Name','SMILES','Formula','MW','Density','IS_J','Td_C','Dv_ms','Hf_kJmol']
df_raw = pd.DataFrame(RAW, columns=COLS)

def parse_formula(formula):
    counts = {}
    for elem in ['C','H','N','O']:
        m = re.search(rf'{elem}(\d*)', str(formula))
        counts[elem] = int(m.group(1)) if m and m.group(1) else (1 if m else 0)
    return counts

fpgen = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=256)

def get_descriptors(row):
    mol = MolFromSmiles(row['SMILES'])
    if mol is None: return None
    e = parse_formula(row['Formula'])
    mw = float(row['MW'])
    ob = (1600/mw)*(2*e['C']+e['H']/2-e['O'])
    fp = fpgen.GetFingerprint(mol)
    arr = np.zeros(256, dtype=np.uint8)
    DataStructs.ConvertToNumpyArray(fp, arr)
    d = {
        'MW': mw, 'nN': e['N'], 'nO': e['O'], 'nC': e['C'],
        'nNO2': row['SMILES'].count('[N+](=O)[O-]'),
        'NC': round(e['N']/(e['C']+1e-9), 3), 'OB': round(ob, 2),
        'TPSA': round(Descriptors.TPSA(mol), 2),
        'LogP': round(Descriptors.MolLogP(mol), 3),
        'HBD': rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumHBD(mol),
        'HBA': rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumHBA(mol),
        'Rings': rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumRings(mol),
        'ArR': rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumAromaticRings(mol),
        'RotB': rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumRotatableBonds(mol),
        'FrCSP3': round(Descriptors.FractionCSP3(mol), 4),
        'Chi0': round(Descriptors.Chi0(mol), 4),
        'Kappa1': round(Descriptors.Kappa1(mol), 4),
        'BalabanJ': round(Descriptors.BalabanJ(mol), 4),
    }
    for i, b in enumerate(arr): d[f'FP{i}'] = int(b)
    return d

# --- 1. Generate Descriptors & Track Valid Rows ---
desc_list = [get_descriptors(row) for _, row in df_raw.iterrows()]

# Create the mask to keep only rows where get_descriptors worked
valid_rows_mask = [bool(d) for d in desc_list]

# Align both DataFrames to the exact same 28 valid rows right here!
df_desc = pd.DataFrame([d for d in desc_list if d])
df_meta = df_raw.loc[valid_rows_mask, [c for c in COLS if c not in ['SMILES','Formula']]].reset_index(drop=True)

# --- 2. Feature Selection & Preprocessing (Now running on aligned 28 rows) ---
vt = VarianceThreshold(0.01)
X_vt = vt.fit_transform(df_desc)
feat_names = df_desc.columns[vt.get_support()].tolist()
X_df = pd.DataFrame(X_vt, columns=feat_names)

corr_mat = X_df.corr().abs()
upper    = corr_mat.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr_mat.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
to_drop  = [c for c in upper.columns if any(upper[c] > 0.92)]
X_clean  = X_df.drop(columns=to_drop)

# --- 3. Scaling (Will correctly output shape: [28, num_features]) ---
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_clean)
feat_names_final = X_clean.columns.tolist()

# --- 4. Pull Out Aligned Target Arrays ---
y_IS  = df_meta['IS_J'].astype(float).values
y_rho = df_meta['Density'].astype(float).values
y_Dv  = df_meta['Dv_ms'].astype(float).values
y_Td  = df_meta['Td_C'].astype(float).values
y_Hf  = df_meta['Hf_kJmol'].astype(float).values
names = df_meta['Name'].values

# --- 5. Verify and Split ---
print(f"X_scaled shape: {X_scaled.shape}") # Expected: (28, n)
print(f"y_IS shape: {y_IS.shape}")         # Expected: (28,)
print(f"names shape: {names.shape}")       # Expected: (28,)

# This will now execute perfectly without errors!
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te, n_tr, n_te = train_test_split(
    X_scaled, y_IS, names, test_size=0.30, random_state=42
)
def evaluate(name, model, Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte):
    model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    p_tr = model.predict(Xtr)
    p_te = model.predict(Xte)
    return {
        'Model': name,
        'R2_train': round(r2_score(ytr, p_tr), 3),
        'R2_test':  round(r2_score(yte, p_te), 3),
        'MAE_test': round(mean_absolute_error(yte, p_te), 2),
        'RMSE_test':round(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yte, p_te)), 2),
    }, model.predict(Xte)

print("B0 ✓ dataset ready:", X_scaled.shape)

    p_tr = model.predict(Xtr)
    p_te = model.predict(Xte)

    }, model.predict(Xte)

def obs_vs_pred(ax, y_obs, y_pred, title, unit=''):
    ax.scatter(y_obs, y_pred, color='steelblue', s=55, alpha=0.8, edgecolors='white')
    lo, hi = min(y_obs.min(), y_pred.min())*0.9, max(y_obs.max(), y_pred.max())*1.05
    ax.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], 'k--', lw=1)
    r2 = r2_score(y_obs, y_pred)
    ax.set_title(f'{title}\nR²={r2:.3f}', fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel(f'Observed {unit}', fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylabel(f'Predicted {unit}', fontsize=8)
    
print('✓ Setup complete')
print("B0 ✓ dataset ready:", X_scaled.shape)

Block 1 · Multiple Linear Regression (MLR)¶

The simplest QSPR model: a weighted sum of descriptors.

$$\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \cdots + w_n x_n$$
Variant When to use
Plain MLR Small datasets, few descriptors, purely linear relationships
Ridge (L2) Many correlated descriptors — shrinks all weights
Lasso (L1) Want automatic feature selection — sets unimportant weights to 0

struct_feats = ['MW','nN','nO','nC','nNO2','NC','OB','TPSA','LogP','HBD','HBA','Rings','ArR','RotB','FrCSP3','Chi0','Kappa1']
struct_feats = [f for f in struct_feats if f in X_clean.columns]
X_struct = scaler.fit_transform(X_clean[struct_feats])
Xs_tr, Xs_te, ys_tr, ys_te = train_test_split(X_struct, y_IS, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)

for name, model in [('MLR', LinearRegression()), 
                    ('Ridge', Ridge(alpha=1.0, solver='svd')), 
                    ('Lasso', Lasso(alpha=0.5, max_iter=5000))]:
    res, _ = evaluate(name, model, Xs_tr, Xs_te, ys_tr, ys_te)
    print(f"B1 {res['Model']}: R2_test={res['R2_test']}")

# ── 1b: MLR coefficients — which descriptors matter most? ─────

mlr_model = LinearRegression().fit(Xs_tr, ys_tr)
coef_df = pd.DataFrame({'Feature': struct_feats,
                         'Coefficient': mlr_model.coef_})\
            .sort_values('Coefficient', key=abs, ascending=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
colors  = ['#e74c3c' if c > 0 else '#3498db' for c in coef_df['Coefficient']]
ax.barh(coef_df['Feature'], coef_df['Coefficient'], color=colors)
ax.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('MLR Coefficient (standardised descriptors)')
ax.set_title('MLR Coefficients for Impact Sensitivity Prediction\n'
             '(red = increases IS,  blue = decreases IS)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print('Intercept:', round(mlr_model.intercept_, 2))
print('\nTop 3 positive (increase sensitivity):',
      coef_df[coef_df['Coefficient']>0].head(3)['Feature'].tolist())
print('Top 3 negative (decrease sensitivity):',
      coef_df[coef_df['Coefficient']<0].head(3)['Feature'].tolist())

Top 3 positive (increase sensitivity): ['MW', 'LogP', 'OB']
Top 3 negative (decrease sensitivity): ['nC', 'nO', 'nN']
In [24]:
# ── 1c: Lasso automatic feature selection ─────────────────────

from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV

lasso_cv = LassoCV(cv=5, max_iter=10000, random_state=42)
lasso_cv.fit(Xs_tr, ys_tr)

non_zero = [(feat, round(coef, 3))
            for feat, coef in zip(struct_feats, lasso_cv.coef_) if coef != 0]
zeroed   = [feat for feat, coef in zip(struct_feats, lasso_cv.coef_) if coef == 0]

print(f'Best alpha (LassoCV): {lasso_cv.alpha_:.4f}')
print(f'Non-zero features kept ({len(non_zero)}): {[f for f,_ in non_zero]}')
print(f'Zeroed out ({len(zeroed)}):               {zeroed}')
r2_lassocv = r2_score(ys_te, lasso_cv.predict(Xs_te))
print(f'LassoCV test R²: {r2_lassocv:.3f}')

Best alpha (LassoCV): 1.9693
Non-zero features kept (5): ['nN', 'nNO2', 'NC', 'HBD', 'FrCSP3']
Zeroed out (9):               ['MW', 'nO', 'nC', 'OB', 'TPSA', 'LogP', 'Rings', 'ArR', 'RotB']
LassoCV test R²: 0.565

Block 2 · Partial Least Squares (PLS)¶

PLS is designed for datasets where descriptors far outnumber compounds and many descriptors are correlated.
It projects both X and y into a smaller set of latent variables that maximise covariance.

Key parameter: n_components — how many latent variables to use.

In [25]:
# ── 2a: PLS — find optimal number of components ───────────────

cv  = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
n_comp_range = range(1, min(10, len(struct_feats)))

cv_r2 = []
for n in n_comp_range:
    pls  = PLSRegression(n_components=n)
    cvsc = cross_val_score(pls, X_struct, y_IS, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
    cv_r2.append(cvsc.mean())

best_n = n_comp_range[int(np.argmax(cv_r2))]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(list(n_comp_range), cv_r2, 'o-', color='steelblue')
ax.axvline(best_n, color='red', linestyle='--', label=f'Best n={best_n}')
ax.set_xlabel('Number of PLS Components')
ax.set_ylabel('5-fold CV R²')
ax.set_title('PLS: Choosing Optimal Number of Components')
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f'Best n_components = {best_n},  CV R² = {cv_r2[best_n-1]:.3f}')

Best n_components = 4,  CV R² = -645226083235968.250
In [26]:
# ── 2b: Fit PLS with best n and evaluate ──────────────────────

pls_best = PLSRegression(n_components=best_n)
res_pls, pred_pls = evaluate('PLS', pls_best, Xs_tr, Xs_te, ys_tr, ys_te)

print('PLS Results:')
for k, v in res_pls.items(): print(f'  {k}: {v}')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4))
obs_vs_pred(ax, ys_te, pred_pls, 'PLS — Impact Sensitivity', 'J')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

  R2_train: 0.754
  R2_test: 0.654
  MAE_test: 15.97
  RMSE_test: 23.25

Block 3 · Support Vector Machine (SVM)¶

SVM finds the best-fitting surface in descriptor space.
The kernel trick lets it capture non-linear relationships without explicitly computing them.

Kernel Relationship captured
linear Straight-line only
rbf (Gaussian) Smooth curved surfaces — most common
poly Polynomial curves

Key parameters: C (how much to penalise errors) and gamma (kernel width).

In [29]:
# ── 3a: Compare SVM kernels ────────────────────────────────────

svm_results = []
for kernel in ['linear', 'rbf', 'poly']:
    res, _ = evaluate(f'SVM ({kernel})',
                      SVR(kernel=kernel, C=10, gamma='scale'),
                      X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te)
    svm_results.append(res)

df_svm = pd.DataFrame(svm_results)
display(df_svm)
Model R2_train R2_test MAE_test RMSE_test
0 SVM (linear) 1.000 0.535 17.22 26.97
1 SVM (rbf) 0.323 0.040 27.48 38.74
2 SVM (poly) 0.382 0.011 30.77 39.32
In [30]:
# ── 3b: Effect of C (regularisation) on SVM performance ───────

C_vals    = [0.01, 0.1, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100]
train_r2s, test_r2s = [], []

for C in C_vals:
    m = SVR(kernel='rbf', C=C, gamma='scale')
    m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    train_r2s.append(r2_score(y_tr, m.predict(X_tr)))
    test_r2s.append(r2_score(y_te,  m.predict(X_te)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.semilogx(C_vals, train_r2s, 'o-', label='Train R²', color='steelblue')
ax.semilogx(C_vals, test_r2s,  's--', label='Test R²',  color='tomato')
ax.set_xlabel('C (log scale)'); ax.set_ylabel('R²')
ax.set_title('SVM (RBF) — Bias-Variance Trade-off as C changes')
ax.legend(); ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print('Low C = underfitting (high bias).  High C = overfitting (high variance).')

Low C = underfitting (high bias).  High C = overfitting (high variance).

Block 4 · Random Forest¶

Random Forest builds many decision trees on random data subsets, then averages predictions.
It is robust, handles non-linearity automatically, and provides feature importance scores.

It is usually the best starting model for energetic materials QSPR.

In [31]:
# ── 4a: Fit Random Forest and show results ─────────────────────

rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
res_rf, pred_rf = evaluate('Random Forest', rf, X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te)

print('Random Forest Results:')
for k, v in res_rf.items(): print(f'  {k}: {v}')

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))

# Observed vs Predicted
obs_vs_pred(axes[0], y_te, pred_rf, 'RF — Impact Sensitivity', 'J')

# Residuals
residuals = y_te - pred_rf
axes[1].scatter(pred_rf, residuals, color='steelblue', s=55, alpha=0.8, edgecolors='white')
axes[1].axhline(0, color='black', lw=1, linestyle='--')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Predicted IS (J)'); axes[1].set_ylabel('Residual (obs − pred)')
axes[1].set_title('Residual Plot — look for random scatter around zero')

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Random Forest Results:

  R2_test: 0.788

Block 5 · Gradient Boosting (XGBoost / sklearn)¶

Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially — each tree corrects errors from the previous.
It typically achieves the highest accuracy on tabular datasets but needs careful tuning.

Parameter What it controls
n_estimators Number of boosting rounds
learning_rate How much each tree contributes (smaller = more robust, needs more trees)
max_depth Depth of each tree (deeper = more complex, more risk of overfit)
subsample Fraction of rows used per tree (< 1 reduces overfit)
In [35]:
# ── 5a: Gradient Boosting — sklearn vs XGBoost ─────────────────

gb_sklearn = GradientBoostingRegressor(
    n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3,
    subsample=0.8, random_state=42)

res_gb, pred_gb = evaluate('GradBoost (sklearn)', gb_sklearn, X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te)

results_boost = [res_gb]

if XGB_OK:
    xgb_model = XGBRegressor(
        n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3,
        subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8,
        random_state=42, verbosity=0)
    res_xgb, pred_xgb = evaluate('XGBoost', xgb_model, X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te)
    results_boost.append(res_xgb)

display(pd.DataFrame(results_boost))
Model R2_train R2_test MAE_test RMSE_test
0 GradBoost (sklearn) 1.0 0.734 13.01 20.42
1 XGBoost 1.0 0.876 10.24 13.94
In [36]:
# ── 5b: Learning curve — training loss vs boosting rounds ──────

# Staged predictions let us watch training and test loss at each round
gb_trace = GradientBoostingRegressor(
    n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3,
    subsample=0.8, random_state=42)
gb_trace.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

train_err = [mean_squared_error(y_tr, pred) for pred in gb_trace.staged_predict(X_tr)]
test_err  = [mean_squared_error(y_te, pred) for pred in gb_trace.staged_predict(X_te)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(train_err, label='Train MSE', color='steelblue')
ax.plot(test_err,  label='Test MSE',  color='tomato')
best_round = int(np.argmin(test_err))
ax.axvline(best_round, color='green', linestyle='--',
           label=f'Best test round = {best_round}')
ax.set_xlabel('Boosting Round'); ax.set_ylabel('MSE')
ax.set_title('Gradient Boosting Learning Curve')
ax.legend(); ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.4)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f'Test MSE bottoms out at round {best_round} — set n_estimators to this.')

Test MSE bottoms out at round 157 — set n_estimators to this.

Block 6 · Cross-Validation — Reliable Performance Estimation¶

A single train/test split gives one number that depends on which compounds land in the test set by chance.
K-fold cross-validation repeats the split K times and averages the result — much more reliable.

Rule: Always report cross-validated performance, not just one test-set R².

In [44]:
# ── 6a: 5-fold and 10-fold CV for all models ──────────────────

models_cv = [
    ('Ridge',          Ridge(alpha=1.0)),
    ('PLS',            PLSRegression(n_components=best_n)),
    ('SVM (RBF)',      SVR(kernel='rbf', C=10, gamma='scale')),
    ('Random Forest',  RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)),
    ('GradBoost',      GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05,
                                                  max_depth=3, random_state=42)),
]

cv_rows = []
for name, model in models_cv:
    cv5  = cross_val_score(model, X_scaled, y_IS, cv=5,  scoring='r2')
    cv10 = cross_val_score(model, X_scaled, y_IS, cv=10, scoring='r2')
    cv_rows.append({
        'Model':         name,
        '5-fold mean':   round(cv5.mean(),  3),
        '5-fold std':    round(cv5.std(),   3),
        '10-fold mean':  round(cv10.mean(), 3),
        '10-fold std':   round(cv10.std(),  3),
    })

df_cv = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows)
display(df_cv)

GradBoost

2 SVM (RBF) -2.660000e-01 5.680000e-01 -3.280100e+01 8.330100e+01
3 Random Forest 2.340000e-01 7.410000e-01 -1.585100e+01 3.746200e+01

Block 7 · Hyperparameter Tuning — Grid Search and Random Search¶

Most models have hyperparameters (settings you choose before training).
Tuning finds the best combination automatically.

Method How it works When to use
Grid Search Tries every combination in a predefined grid Small grids (<100 combos)
Random Search Randomly samples combinations Large grids — often finds good settings faster
In [54]:
# ── 7a: Grid search — SVM ─────────────────────────────────────

svm_grid = {
    'C':     [0.1, 1, 10, 50],
    'gamma': ['scale', 0.01, 0.001],
    'kernel':['rbf', 'linear'],
}

gs = GridSearchCV(SVR(), svm_grid, cv=5, scoring='r2', n_jobs=-1, verbose=0)
gs.fit(X_scaled, y_IS)

print('Grid Search — SVM')
print(f'  Best params: {gs.best_params_}')
print(f'  Best CV R²:  {gs.best_score_:.3f}')

# Show top 5 combinations
cv_results = pd.DataFrame(gs.cv_results_)\
               .sort_values('mean_test_score', ascending=False)\
               [['param_C','param_gamma','param_kernel','mean_test_score','std_test_score']]\
               .head(5)
cv_results.columns = ['C','gamma','kernel','mean_R2','std_R2']
display(cv_results)

# ── 7b: Random search — Random Forest ─────────────────────────

from scipy.stats import randint, uniform

rf_param_dist = {
    'n_estimators':      randint(50, 400),
    'max_depth':         [None, 3, 5, 8, 10],
    'min_samples_split': randint(2, 10),
    'min_samples_leaf':  randint(1, 5),
    'max_features':      ['sqrt', 'log2', 0.5],
}

rs = RandomizedSearchCV(
    RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    rf_param_dist, n_iter=30, cv=5,
    scoring='r2', random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, verbose=0)
rs.fit(X_scaled, y_IS)

print('Random Search — Random Forest')
print(f'  Best params: {rs.best_params_}')
print(f'  Best CV R²:  {rs.best_score_:.3f}')

# Plot improvement over iterations
rs_df = pd.DataFrame(rs.cv_results_).sort_values('rank_test_score')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.scatter(range(len(rs_df)), rs_df['mean_test_score'], s=30, alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(rs.best_score_, color='red', linestyle='--',
           label=f'Best R²={rs.best_score_:.3f}')
ax.set_xlabel('Iteration rank (best to worst)')
ax.set_ylabel('5-fold CV R²')
ax.set_title('Random Search — Random Forest (30 iterations)')
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Block 8 · Model Comparison Dashboard¶

Compare all models side-by-side on the same dataset using the same split.
Use CV R² as the primary metric — not training R².

In [61]:
# ── 8a: Train all models and collect metrics ──────────────────

best_svm = gs.best_estimator_
best_rf  = rs.best_estimator_




final_models = [
    # Change solver to 'svd' or 'sag' to avoid the sym_pos error
    ('Ridge',         Ridge(alpha=1.0, solver='svd')), 
    ('PLS',           PLSRegression(n_components=best_n)),
    ('SVM (tuned)',   best_svm),
    ('RF (tuned)',    best_rf),
    ('GradBoost',     GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05,
                                                max_depth=3, random_state=42)),
]



dashboard_rows = []
pred_all = {}
for name, model in final_models:
    cv5  = cross_val_score(model, X_scaled, y_IS, cv=5, scoring='r2')
    res, pred = evaluate(name, model, X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te)
    res['CV5_mean'] = round(cv5.mean(), 3)
    res['CV5_std']  = round(cv5.std(),  3)
    dashboard_rows.append(res)
    pred_all[name]  = pred

df_dash = pd.DataFrame(dashboard_rows)
display(df_dash)

In [63]:
# ── 8c: Radar comparison chart ────────────────────────────────

import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

metrics    = ['R2_train','R2_test','CV5_mean']
inv_metrics= ['MAE_test','RMSE_test']   # lower=better → invert for radar

# Normalise 0-1 for radar
radar_df = df_dash.set_index('Model')[metrics + inv_metrics].copy()
for col in inv_metrics:   # invert so bigger = better
    radar_df[col] = 1 - (radar_df[col] - radar_df[col].min()) / \
                        (radar_df[col].max() - radar_df[col].min() + 1e-9)
for col in metrics:
    radar_df[col] = (radar_df[col] - radar_df[col].min()) / \
                    (radar_df[col].max() - radar_df[col].min() + 1e-9)

all_labels = metrics + [f'1/({m})' for m in inv_metrics]
angles = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, len(all_labels), endpoint=False).tolist()
angles += angles[:1]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6), subplot_kw=dict(polar=True))
colors_r = plt.cm.Set2.colors

for idx, (model_name, row) in enumerate(radar_df.iterrows()):
    vals = row.tolist() + row.tolist()[:1]
    ax.plot(angles, vals, 'o-', lw=1.8, color=colors_r[idx], label=model_name)
    ax.fill(angles, vals, alpha=0.1, color=colors_r[idx])

ax.set_thetagrids(np.degrees(angles[:-1]), all_labels, fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title('Model Comparison Radar\n(all axes: higher = better)', fontsize=11, pad=20)
ax.legend(loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.4, 1.15), fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Block 9 · Predict All Properties¶

Chapter 4 covers five prediction targets.
Here we train the best model (Random Forest) separately for each property
and plot all observed-vs-predicted results together.

In [65]:
# ── 9a: Train RF for each property ────────────────────────────

targets = {
    'Impact Sensitivity (J)':    y_IS,
    'Crystal Density (g/cc)':    y_rho,
    'Detonation Velocity (m/s)': y_Dv,
    'Decomp. Temperature (°C)':  y_Td,
    'Heat of Formation (kJ/mol)':y_Hf,
}

prop_results = []
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(14, 8))
axes = axes.flatten()

for idx, (label, y_prop) in enumerate(targets.items()):
    Xp_tr, Xp_te, yp_tr, yp_te = train_test_split(
        X_scaled, y_prop, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)

    rf_prop = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
    rf_prop.fit(Xp_tr, yp_tr)
    yp_pred = rf_prop.predict(Xp_te)

    r2  = r2_score(yp_te, yp_pred)
    mae = mean_absolute_error(yp_te, yp_pred)
    prop_results.append({'Property': label,
                          'R2_test': round(r2, 3),
                          'MAE_test': round(mae, 2)})

    ax = axes[idx]
    obs_vs_pred(ax, yp_te, yp_pred, label.split('(')[0].strip())

axes[-1].axis('off')   # hide unused 6th subplot
plt.suptitle('Random Forest — All Property Predictions (Test Set)',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

display(pd.DataFrame(prop_results))

# ── 9b: Kamlet-Jacobs vs ML — detonation velocity ─────────────
# Compare empirical KJ equations with RF predictions

def kamlet_jacobs_D(N, M, Q, rho):
    phi = N * math.sqrt(M * Q)
    return round(1.01 * math.sqrt(phi) * (1 + 1.30*rho) * 1000, 0)

# KJ parameters for the 4 compounds we have data for
kj_known = {
    'TNT':  (0.01987, 50.51, 1080, 1.654),
    'RDX':  (0.02987, 27.67, 1510, 1.820),
    'HMX':  (0.02975, 27.61, 1482, 1.905),
    'PETN': (0.02865, 28.26, 1510, 1.778),
}

comp_rows = []
for cname, (N, M, Q, rho) in kj_known.items():
    idx  = list(names).index(cname)
    rf_d = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
    rf_d.fit(X_scaled, y_Dv)
    rf_pred = round(rf_d.predict(X_scaled[[idx]])[0], 0)
    comp_rows.append({
        'Compound':   cname,
        'Experimental': df_meta.loc[df_meta['Name']==cname, 'Dv_ms'].values[0],
        'KJ Estimate':  kamlet_jacobs_D(N, M, Q, rho),
        'RF Predicted': rf_pred,
    })

df_kj_vs_rf = pd.DataFrame(comp_rows)
df_kj_vs_rf['KJ Error %'] = abs(df_kj_vs_rf['KJ Estimate'] - df_kj_vs_rf['Experimental'])\
                              / df_kj_vs_rf['Experimental'] * 100
df_kj_vs_rf['RF Error %'] = abs(df_kj_vs_rf['RF Predicted'] - df_kj_vs_rf['Experimental'])\
                              / df_kj_vs_rf['Experimental'] * 100
df_kj_vs_rf[['KJ Error %','RF Error %']] = df_kj_vs_rf[['KJ Error %','RF Error %']].round(1)

display(df_kj_vs_rf)

Block 10 · Domain of Applicability (DoA)¶

A QSPR model is only reliable for molecules similar to its training set.
The domain of applicability tells you when NOT to trust a prediction.

Three methods covered:

  1. Leverage (hat values) — distance from training data centroid in descriptor space
  2. Euclidean distance to nearest training compound
  3. Prediction interval — how much the forest's trees disagree
In [67]:
# ── 10a: Leverage method ───────────────────────────────────────
# h = x^T (X^T X)^{-1} x
# Warning threshold: h* = 3(p+1)/n   where p=features, n=train samples

from numpy.linalg import pinv

# Use structural descriptors only for interpretability
struct_idx = [i for i, f in enumerate(feat_names_final)
              if not f.startswith('FP')]
Xs_tr_doa  = X_tr[:, struct_idx]
Xs_te_doa  = X_te[:, struct_idx]
Xs_all_doa = X_scaled[:, struct_idx]

H_matrix = Xs_tr_doa @ pinv(Xs_tr_doa.T @ Xs_tr_doa) @ Xs_tr_doa.T
h_train  = np.diag(H_matrix)

# Leverage for test set
p  = Xs_tr_doa.shape[1]
n  = Xs_tr_doa.shape[0]
h_star = 3 * (p + 1) / n

h_test = np.array([
    float(x @ pinv(Xs_tr_doa.T @ Xs_tr_doa) @ x)
    for x in Xs_te_doa
])

rf_doa = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
rf_doa.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
pred_doa = rf_doa.predict(X_te)
std_res  = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_tr, rf_doa.predict(X_tr)))
std_res  = max(std_res, 1e-6)
s_test   = (y_te - pred_doa) / std_res

print(f'Warning threshold h* = {h_star:.3f}')
print(f'Test compounds with h > h*: '
      f'{[n_te[i] for i in range(len(h_test)) if h_test[i] > h_star]}')

# Williams plot: leverage vs standardised residual
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.scatter(h_train, np.zeros(len(h_train)), s=40, color='steelblue',
           label='Training', alpha=0.6)
ax.scatter(h_test, s_test, s=70, color='tomato',
           label='Test', alpha=0.9, edgecolors='white')
for i, name in enumerate(n_te):
    ax.annotate(name, (h_test[i], s_test[i]),
                textcoords='offset points', xytext=(5, 3), fontsize=7)

ax.axvline(h_star, color='green', linestyle='--', label=f'h* = {h_star:.2f}')
ax.axhline(3,  color='grey',  linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8)
ax.axhline(-3, color='grey',  linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Leverage (h)')
ax.set_ylabel('Standardised Residual')
ax.set_title('Williams Plot — Domain of Applicability\n'
             'Right of green line = outside DoA.  |y|>3 = outlier prediction.')
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# ── 10b: Euclidean distance to nearest training neighbour ──────

from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances

dist_matrix = pairwise_distances(X_te, X_tr)
min_dist    = dist_matrix.min(axis=1)   # distance to nearest training compound

# Threshold = 95th percentile of training-set internal distances
train_self_dist = pairwise_distances(X_tr, X_tr)
np.fill_diagonal(train_self_dist, np.nan)
thresh_dist = np.nanpercentile(train_self_dist, 95)

doa_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Compound':     n_te,
    'Min_dist':     min_dist.round(3),
    'Observed IS':  y_te,
    'Predicted IS': pred_doa.round(1),
    'In DoA':       min_dist < thresh_dist
})

print(f'Distance threshold (95th pct): {thresh_dist:.3f}')
display(doa_df)

# ── 10c: Prediction interval from RF tree disagreement ─────────
# Each tree in RF gives a prediction; std across trees = confidence

tree_preds = np.array([tree.predict(X_te) for tree in rf_doa.estimators_])
pred_mean  = tree_preds.mean(axis=0)
pred_std   = tree_preds.std(axis=0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
x_pos = np.arange(len(n_te))
ax.bar(x_pos, pred_mean, color='steelblue', alpha=0.7, label='RF prediction')
ax.errorbar(x_pos, pred_mean, yerr=2*pred_std, fmt='none',
            color='black', capsize=4, label='±2σ (95% interval)')
ax.scatter(x_pos, y_te, color='red', zorder=5, s=60, label='Observed')
ax.set_xticks(x_pos)
ax.set_xticklabels(n_te, rotation=30, ha='right', fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel('Impact Sensitivity (J)')
ax.set_title('RF Prediction Intervals (±2σ from tree disagreement)\n'
             'Wide bars = high uncertainty = treat prediction with caution')
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
